transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. Welcome in—what brings you here to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, it's... well, it's a bit of a story, to be honest with you. See, it all started at the county fair this past weekend. I was there, representing the agricultural association, like I do most years, and I was giving this talk. A very important talk, mind you, about crop rotation and the new seasonal yields. And, well, the crowd was there, standing around the John Deere display, and I just... I had to show them. It wasn't enough to just tell them, you know? I had to demonstrate the energy of it, the movement. So, I climbed right up onto the biggest tractor they had out there. It was a beautiful machine, brand new, and I got up in the cab and I just started working the controls. I was jerking them back and forth, really putting my back into it, trying to show them the 'new pattern.' The pattern that’s going to change everything, you see? And the thing is, I knew it was making a scene. People were staring, and then the fair organizers, they started yelling at me to get down. Shouting, really. But I couldn't. I just couldn't make myself stop. My hands were on those levers and I was locked in, showing them the pattern, even with all that hollering. Next thing I know, security is there, and my family is all in a panic, and well... that's why they brought me in to see you today. They think I made a fool of myself, but I was just trying to show them...
Can you tell me how many days or weeks you've been feeling this way—full of energy, excited, and unable to stop yourself—before the fair incident happened?

Well, now, that’s just it, Dr. Smith. People look at the fair and they think, 'Oh, he just got a little carried away on a Saturday afternoon.' They think it’s a sudden thing, a matter of a few days or maybe a week of getting too excited. But that’s not the truth of it at all. If you really want to know the timeline, if we’re being exact about it... well, you have to look at the whole calendar. 

Because these stretches—these incredibly charged, completely sleepless, just absolutely nonstop stretches—they haven't just been a few weeks. I’d say they’ve taken up about ten months of this past year or so. Ten months! 

It goes all the way back to last fall, right in the thick of the harvest. I’d be out in the machine shed at two, three in the morning, tearing down the combine engine and putting it back together, or reorganizing the entire feed system, because I just didn't need to close my eyes. My body was just humming with it. I'd be out walking the property lines in the pitch dark, feeling that exact same excitement I had at the fair, just knowing exactly how the soil was shifting and what needed to be done. My family, they'd come out and tell me to come to bed, saying I was working too hard, but they didn't understand that I couldn't stop if I tried. The engine was just running too hot, too good. It’s just been this massive, rolling wave of energy for ten solid months out of the year, day in and day out, right up until I climbed up into that John Deere cab...
Before this stretch of high energy started, have you ever gone through a period—weeks or more—where you felt very down, lost interest in things, or had low energy and low mood?

Well, down? Lost interest? No, Dr. Smith, I... I can't rightly say I've ever been the type to just lay around and lose interest in things. I mean, if you really think about it, how could I? When you're managing a working farm—when you've got equipment to maintain, and the weather dictating your every move, and crops that absolutely do not wait for you to decide if you're in a good mood or a bad mood—you just don't have the luxury of losing interest. The land doesn't care if you're feeling a bit low, you see? It demands your attention. 

Now, sure, maybe years ago, long before all this current energy kicked in, maybe I'd get tired after a long day of baling hay in the August heat. Anyone would! You come in, you take your boots off by the mudroom door, you're exhausted, your bones ache a bit—I'm sixty years old, I'm not exactly a spring chicken anymore. But that's just honest fatigue. That's just the body saying it's done for the day. That's entirely different from being down in the dumps or not wanting to do it all over again the next morning. 

I always wake up ready to go. I've always been a doer. My father was a worker, his father before him... we just keep moving, it's in our blood. So, no, I haven't ever had a stretch of weeks where I just couldn't get out of bed or didn't care about the property. Even before this past year, before this... this current engine inside me got revved up so incredibly high, I was just going about my business, steady as a rock. I don't really get sad or low like some folks do. I mean, my wife, she watches those programs on the television sometimes where people are crying and talking about their feelings and how they can't face the day, but that's just never made a lick of sense to me. I've always got a project, always got a fence line that needs walking or a ledger that needs balancing. So, no, none of that low energy, depressed stuff for me. I just haven't ever had that happen.

During this period of high energy, have you believed you had special powers, a unique mission, or important abilities that others don't have—or have you seen or heard things that others couldn't see or hear?

Well, Dr. Smith, that’s... that’s a very interesting question. Because, you see, when you’re out there, and the energy is just pouring through you, and you’re awake for days on end, pushing the expansion, working the fields... things start to become clear. Very clear. It’s not about special powers like in a comic book or something silly like that. It’s about being tuned in. 

I mean, during those months—and like I said, it was ten solid months of just pushing, pushing, pushing, getting the new acreage cleared, working day and night when I hardly needed to close my eyes for more than an hour—I started noticing things that other folks just walk right past. For instance, the irrigation lines. Now, most people just hear water running through aluminum pipes, right? A hum, a rattle. But I started hearing... well, voices. It wasn't just water. It was distinct, rhythmic voices coming right out of the pipes, telling me exactly when the pressure was off, whispering about the water table, giving me instructions on how to route the flow to maximize the root systems. It was clear as day to me, even if my wife just thought it was the pump acting up.

And it wasn't just the water, either. The yield maps! You know those digital maps the new combines spit out? The ones that show the high and low production areas in different colors? I’d be sitting in the office at 3:00 AM, looking at those printouts, and the colors... they weren't just data anymore. They were forming patterns, actual warnings. I could read them like a book. They were spelling out exactly which sections of the north quarter were going to fail if I didn't intervene immediately. It was a direct message, a warning that only I could decipher because I was the one awake, I was the one doing the work. So, I wouldn't call it a 'special power,' exactly, but I was definitely hearing and seeing the truth of the land in a way that nobody else around here could even begin to understand.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient exhibits a prolonged (~10 month) period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive mood with markedly increased energy, decreased need for sleep, excessive involvement in goal-directed activities (farm work, mechanical projects), grandiosity (belief he is uniquely 'tuned in' to the land), and risky/disinhibited behavior with impaired judgment (climbing onto tractor, ignoring warnings from authorities) causing severe functional impairment. During this manic period, he also reports mood-congruent psychotic symptoms—auditory hallucinations ('voices' from irrigation pipes) and delusional beliefs (yield map 'warnings' only he can decipher)—consistent with mania with psychotic features. He denies any prior or concurrent depressive episodes, ruling out bipolar I with mixed/depressive features as the primary presentation for this episode, and the psychotic symptoms are entirely mood-congruent and confined to the manic period, arguing against a primary psychotic disorder (e.g., schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder). This is coded as a single manic episode with psychotic symptoms (F30.2); if this were a recurrence within a known bipolar disorder, F31.2 would apply, and this remains a close differential pending longitudinal history.
